analysis.one_liner: Makes it a crime for former members of Congress to lobby their old colleagues at any time.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Judiciary Committee and one of its subcommittees until the Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would replace today's cooling-off rules, which let former senators lobby after two years and former House members after one, with a permanent criminal ban: a former senator or representative could never make a lobbying contact with any member, officer, or employee of Congress or senior executive branch officials. Violations would carry criminal fines and possible prison time under existing federal penalty provisions. Former elected House officers, such as the Speaker or Clerk, would face a one-year ban. The rules would apply to anyone leaving office after the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens, who would gain a firewall against former lawmakers cashing in on their relationships to steer legislation and policy toward paying clients.

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the current one-year (House) and two-year (Senate) waiting periods with an outright, lifetime ban on lobbying contacts by former members of Congress, enforced with criminal fines and imprisonment [S2] [S3].
Extends the ban to contacts with senior executive branch officials as well as members and staff of both chambers, closing the main routes a former lawmaker would use to sell influence [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Former members of Congress, who would permanently lose a lucrative career path, and the lobbying firms and industries that hire them for their access to former colleagues.
analysis.who_pays_short: Former lawmakers and their lobbying clients

drawbacks.text: A lifetime criminal ban would apply to every departing member regardless of role, and critics of revolving-door restrictions have long argued that such bans can go too far, blocking former officials from legitimate work advising on matters they never touched and potentially driving policy expertise out of government; the bill text contains no exception for unpaid, pro-bono, or representational activity beyond the standard exemptions imported from the Lobbying Disclosure Act definitions [S3].

Because violations are criminal, enforcement questions would arise about what counts as a 'lobbying contact' in ordinary professional life, since the bill adopts the broad definitions of the Lobbying Disclosure Act rather than a narrow trading-on-insider-relationships standard [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit, closing the revolving door that turns congressional service into a lobbying career, is real and widely supported by ethics advocates. The honest cost is that a blanket lifetime criminal ban is blunt: it sweeps in departing members who never had special influence and contains no carve-outs for benign work, so a narrower ban tied to matters the member actually handled would be a more surgical design. Still, the public benefit of making member-to-lobbyist conversion illegal is substantial.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which passed it along to the Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security subcommittee, and neither ever scheduled a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. David Cicilline introduced the bill on November 18, 2011, during the first session of the 112th Congress [S1] [S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary on the day of introduction [S5].
On December 2, 2011, it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security [S5].
No further action was taken, and the bill received no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Lobbying firms and the industries that hire former members of Congress kept the existing one- and two-year waiting periods, which allow lawmakers to move into lobbying careers almost immediately after leaving office. Incumbent members of both parties are also better off, since the option of a future lobbying career remains open.

for.name: Rep. David Cicilline
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its sole advocate in the record.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only cosponsor it attracted.

against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee and never scheduled a hearing or markup during the two-year Congress.

against.name: House of Representatives
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor for debate or a vote at any point in the 112th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The record shows only two Democrats, the sponsor and one cosponsor; no Republican supported the bill and no vote was ever taken, so partisan lines were never tested.

industries.note: The bill would cut off their ability to recruit former senators and representatives, whose access to sitting colleagues is their most valuable asset. Had it passed, the industry would have lost its easiest source of insider hires; because it died, that pipeline stayed open.

industries.industry: Regulated industries that hire former lawmakers (finance, pharmaceuticals, defense, energy)
industries.note: These employers buy former members for their relationships and procedural knowledge. A lifetime ban would have made that purchase far less valuable.

industries.industry: Incumbent members of Congress as a class
industries.note: The bill would have imposed a direct career cost on every sitting member, converting a future lobbying payday into a criminal act. Members of both parties had a personal stake in keeping it buried.
